walkthroughs.body_html:
Wave Phenomena — a core area of Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Wave Phenomena brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Wave Phenomena.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Why does light bend when it enters a denser medium like glass?
options: Fission combines small atoms into bigger ones, and fusion splits them.
Because gravity in the glass pulls the light down.
Because it slows down — the change in speed at the boundary causes the wavefront to bend (towards the normal).
Because the medium is denser, it physically blocks part of the light and forces it to turn.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between nuclear fission and fusion?
options: Fission combines small atoms into bigger ones, and fusion splits them.
Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones; fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier one.
Fission and fusion are the same process, just at different scales.
Yes, but only in cities with old buildings.

mcqs.q: Is background radiation always present, even when no source is being studied?
options: Yes — natural sources (rocks, cosmic rays, food) produce a low level of radiation everywhere on Earth.
No — background radiation only appears near nuclear power stations.
Yes, but only in cities with old buildings.
Because gravity in the glass pulls the light down.
